transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-10
Start: 08:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Alvarez (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (StratusTel Cloud Architect), Lisa Nguyen (StratusTel Head of Security), Marco Silvestri (Network Eng), Karen O'Leary (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood overview of Private deployment options (VPC peering vs private endpoints vs dedicated in-region). Customer constraints: data residency in eu-west-1 + us-east-1, strict egress controls, need for audit logs and KMS integration. Agreement to share network diagrams and follow-up technical deep dive.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, i'm the AE on this account, quick intros?
[00:06] Raj Patel: yeah hi, i'm raj, cloud arch, i run our internal infra for ml platforms, thanks for making time
[00:10] Lisa Nguyen: lisa here, head of security at stratustel
[00:13] Marco Silvestri: marco, network eng, i'll be owning the peering and firewall rules side
[00:16] Karen O'Leary: karen, procurement, hi
[00:18] Tom Alvarez: tom, se at redwood, i'll cover the deep tech bits on peering and private endpoints
[00:22] Maya Chen: awesome, goal for today is to understand your networking and region constraints and map the best private deployment path — whether hosted with private endpoints, dedicated pools in our region, or a private control plane in your vpc. not trying to sell, just figure out constraints.

[00:37] Raj Patel: main things for us: we run across eu-west-1 for customer data residency, and us-east-1 for compute flexibility. we need traffic to stay inside our network where possible, and if egress happens it's logged, and ideally to our egress gateways. we also want to avoid internet-facing endpoints for inference.
[00:53] Lisa Nguyen: and we require audit logs retained for 1 year, SSO via okta, scoping for kms and hsm integrations, and proof of SOC2 compliance.
[01:02] Tom Alvarez: totally get it. we have three common patterns: vpc peering to our private subnets with peered routing, private endpoints (endpoint services) where traffic goes over aws private link or equivalents, or a private deployment where the control plane is customer-hosted and models run inside your vpc. each has tradeoffs.
[01:21] Marco Silvestri: can you go into the peering tradeoffs? we already have lots of peering with partners, but routing and asymmetric paths are our headache.
[01:29] Tom Alvarez: yeah, sure. peering is straightforward if you want low-latency and you trust route tables; it's just VPC peering or transit gateway. drawbacks: with peering you need to manage route propagation, and cross-account security groups, and we sometimes need to coordinate MTU and path MTU issues — also no transitive peering unless you use a TGW. private endpoints via AWS PrivateLink avoid route table sprawl, since you create an endpoint service in our account and you create an interface endpoint on your side; that gives you more control on egress but can cost more per-hour per-endpoint and has ENI scaling considerations.
[02:05] Raj Patel: okay, ENI scaling — what's typical for high throughput inference? we have bursty traffic, sometimes spikes during nights for batch scoring.
[02:14] Tom Alvarez: with private endpoints we recommend pinning to a dedicated pool and enabling autoscaling policies; ENI counts scale with connections, so for heavy QPS you want a few endpoints in different AZs. for dedicated we can co-locate GPUs in the same region to minimize cross-AZ costs. if you do private control plane (on-prem or vpc) you avoid cross-account ENIs but you take on the control plane ops.
[02:36] Lisa Nguyen: what about cross-region restrictions — our legal team requires that EU customer data never leaves eu-west-1. we may want a dedicated deployment in eu-west-1 only.
[02:45] Maya Chen: that's doable. many customers have a regional dedicated pool. we can offer dedicated capacity in eu-west-1 and a separate pool in us-east-1 for internal models if you prefer. the key is model sync and versioning: we ship model artifacts to the region you choose or you can bring-your-own-model with model registry mirroring.
[03:03] Marco Silvestri: on the networking side, we need to know the NAT egress footprints, IP ranges you will present so we can lock down outbound rules to egress gateways. can you provide a list?
[03:12] Tom Alvarez: yes we can provide a set of egress IP ranges per region; note those ranges are sometimes per-cluster and may change with scaling but we provide a published prefix list and endpoint IP ranges for private endpoints. we'll send the CIDR lists and recommended firewall rules.
[03:27] Raj Patel: also do you support VPC peering via AWS TGW? we already use a transit gateway and prefer attaching there rather than pairwise peering.
[03:34] Tom Alvarez: yes, TGW is supported. we can attach to a TGW via a VPC backend or you can establish an inter-region peering at the TGW level; we typically exchange a couple of routes and set up BGP with customers that use Direct Connect — if you have DX we'll map the routes.
[03:50] Lisa Nguyen: encryption at rest — does redwood support CMEK with our KMS keys for private deployments?
[03:56] Tom Alvarez: for private and dedicated we support customer-managed keys (CMEK) for model artifact storage and encryption of persistent cache layers. HSM-level integrations are available via our enterprise package; we can share the KMS integration guide.
[04:10] Marco Silvestri: what about VPC endpoints for object storage — do you use s3 endpoints or do you require internet egress to pull model blobs?
[04:16] Tom Alvarez: we can use S3 VPC endpoints or object-store equivalents; for hosted flows model pulls can be done via signed URLs through private endpoints, or for private deployments you can host the model inside your S3 and we access it over the VPC endpoints. no need for internet egress if we set up the right endpoint service.
[04:31] Maya Chen: quick question, procurement timeline? karen?
[04:34] Karen O'Leary: we're on a Q1 procurement window, budget sign-off likely mid-march, but vendor security docs need to go to legal ASAP. we'll need SOC2, pen test reports, and an initial SOW for dedicated capacity.
[04:45] Maya Chen: noted. i'll upload SOC2 and pen test summary and a templated SOW.
[04:48] Lisa Nguyen: we also want to clarify retention for audit logs — can logs be exported to our SIEM in real time?
[04:54] Tom Alvarez: yes, we have log forwarding via Kinesis/CloudWatch export or syslog to your SIEM, and we can push structured events for every inference request including token counts and model version metadata. there's a bit of PII concern so we can redact request bodies at the token level if you need.
[05:13] Raj Patel: about latency — if we run models in eu-west-1 and our app is in us-east-1, we see network latency. what's the best practice there?
[05:20] Tom Alvarez: best is regionalizing inference near the user or using a hybrid: serve sensitive customer data in eu-west-1 and run non-sensitive models in us-east-1. smart routing lets you pin models to regions and do fallback to lower-cost region if latency SLOs aren't met. for stateful chat workloads KV cache locality matters; cache warming can reduce p95 significantly.
[05:40] Marco Silvestri: are there any implications for TLS termination when using private endpoints? we prefer TLS to terminate in our VPC.
[05:46] Tom Alvarez: for PrivateLink endpoints TLS is mutual TLS by default between the ENI and our service, but if you want TLS to terminate inside your VPC, we can support client-side certs and a TLS passthrough pattern if you run a private control plane. it's more advanced but doable.
[06:03] Lisa Nguyen: ok, auditability and key management sound fine but we need to see the whitepaper.
[06:08] Maya Chen: we'll attach the whitepaper. one more thing — do you have any performance numbers for quantized models behind private endpoints?
[06:15] Tom Alvarez: yes, we have benchmarks across quantization levels and sequence lengths — we'll share a short perf sheet showing p50/p95 for tps and latency in eu-west-1 vs us-east-1 on similar GPU configs. expect slightly higher latency when you do private link due to ENI hops, but usually within single-digit ms for optimized kernels.
[06:35] Raj Patel: any compliance gotchas for cross-account peering? our legal is cautious about shared infra.
[06:41] Maya Chen: we often sign data processing addenda and can put the control plane SLA and data residency clauses into the contract. for dedicated you get physical separation in terms of capacity pools and audit logs per-customer.
[06:53] Marco Silvestri: i have a question on MTU — we had fragmentation issues with other vendors when large payloads hit inference endpoints. how do you handle jumbo frames?
[07:01] Tom Alvarez: we support standard MTU and can tune path MTU and advise on TCP MSS clamping. typically reassembling large requests at the application layer helps, and we recommend chunking big prompt blobs. we'll include recommended tcp/ip tuning in the peering checklist.
[07:18] Raj Patel: are there limits to number of subnets or endpoints per AZ we need to know?
[07:24] Tom Alvarez: there are cloud provider limits: ENI counts per instance and endpoints per AZ may hit soft limits; we document recommended quotas and autoscaling knobs. if you have very large QPS we recommend a dedicated pool with multiple endpoint interfaces spread across AZs.
[07:38] Karen O'Leary: procurement question — if we sign for dedicated capacity in eu-west-1, what's typical lead time for provisioning?
[07:44] Maya Chen: for dedicated it's about 2–4 weeks depending on capacity sizing and contract, sometimes faster if we have standing inventory. private control plane deployments take longer — often 4–8 weeks with network validation.
[07:57] Marco Silvestri: can you do an initial pilot with limited throughput so we can validate peering?
[08:01] Maya Chen: yes, pilot is standard — we can spin up a small dedicated pool or a hosted private endpoint with limited qps for testing.
[08:07] Raj Patel: we'd like to run an internal benchmark: a 5k qps-ish batch scoring test and a chat p95 target of 200ms in-region. possible?
[08:16] Tom Alvarez: 200ms p95 for chat depends on model size; for small to medium models yes, for large 30B+ it's harder. for batch 5k qps we recommend batching and autoscaling and a dedicated pool. we'll map the exact GPU count after we see profiles.
[08:32] Lisa Nguyen: one last security question — do you have an allowlist of personnel access to customer data? we need a SOC2-style org map.
[08:38] Maya Chen: yes we can provide a data-access roster and verifier; that's part of our security pack.
[08:43] Tom Alvarez: ok i think we have the network items we need to produce: peering checklist, CIDR/egress ranges, terraform snippets, endpoint ENI scaling guidance.
[08:51] Maya Chen: recap and next steps — i'll send SOC2, pen test summary, SOW template, and initial pricing options by friday. tom will send the peering checklist and terraform examples by thursday. raj will upload topology and IP ranges tomorrow. schedule deep dive with marco for next week?
[09:05] Raj Patel: next week works, maybe thursday morning our time
[09:08] Karen O'Leary: we'll also need a redline-friendly SOW for procurement
[09:11] Maya Chen: noted — i'll include a redlineable SOW and procurement checklist. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the calendar.
[09:17] End of call.
